title: Trump: Science of sex and gender being misrepresented by Trump officials, experts warn
description_short: Trump: Science of sex and gender being misrepresented by Trump officials, experts warn
description_medium: Science of sex and gender being misrepresented by Trump officials, experts warn. Scientists say crackdown on gender-affirming care could have impact on healthcare of all Americans This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long:
On February 27, 2026, reporting described a Department of Health and Human Services rule in development that would block Medicaid and Medicare payments to health systems providing gender-affirming care to patients under 18. The public comment period had ended the week before; the article described a proposal, not a final rule. It also reported that several major clinics had ended pediatric gender-affirming care programs during the administration’s broader crackdown.

The article quoted Jey McCreight, a human-genomics researcher, and Jess McLaughlin, a biological-sciences professor at the University of Alaska Anchorage. Both said officials and policy makers were presenting sex and gender science too simplistically. McLaughlin noted that chromosomes, hormones, anatomy and other traits do not always align in a strict binary. McCreight said claims used to restrict care depart from biological evidence.

The report also described restrictions on gender-affirming care in federal prisons, including limits on hormones, clothing and non-surgical services. The proposed funding rule and prison policies put youth treatment and adult care under pressure. The two experts warned that scientific claims used to limit transgender health services could shape decisions about healthcare more broadly.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

title: Trump administration meets with UK far-right activist Tommy Robinson
description_short: Trump administration meets with UK far-right activist Tommy Robinson
description_medium: Trump administration meets with UK far-right activist Tommy Robinson. Agitator whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon was hosted by senior adviser at US state department This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long:
On February 25, 2026, Tommy Robinson, a British far-right activist whose legal name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, visited the State Department in Washington. Senior adviser Joe Rittenhouse hosted him and posted photographs from the department’s John Quincy Adams State Drawing Room. Rittenhouse called Robinson a “free speech warrior” and framed the meeting around freedom of speech. Robinson wrote that he had been invited to the department.

A State Department spokesperson told Reuters that Robinson was visiting in an “unofficial capacity” on a tour. The spokesperson did not answer questions about who else he met, what was discussed or the objective of the visit. The article also noted Robinson’s convictions and legal cases, and reported that he had recently said he left the United Kingdom after police warned him of a threat to his safety.

The meeting drew criticism from Scottish Green MSP Maggie Chapman, who said the administration’s welcome of Robinson was alarming. The public posts show how Rittenhouse and Robinson described the contact; the department characterized it as an unofficial tour. Its agenda and any policy discussion were not disclosed.

title: Trump: Environmental groups sue Trump’s EPA over repeal of landmark climate finding
description_short: Trump: Environmental groups sue Trump’s EPA over repeal of landmark climate finding
description_medium: Environmental groups sue Trump’s EPA over repeal of landmark climate finding. Lawsuit from health and environmental justice groups challenges the EPA’s rollback of the ‘endangerment finding’ This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long:
On February 18, 2026, more than a dozen health and environmental groups sued the Environmental Protection Agency in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit after the agency revoked the endangerment finding. The 2009 determination treats greenhouse-gas pollution as a threat to public health and welfare and has supported federal limits on emissions from vehicles, power plants and other industries. The plaintiffs included the American Public Health Association, American Lung Association, Center for Biological Diversity, Environmental Defense Fund, Natural Resources Defense Council and Sierra Club. Earthjustice and Clean Air Task Force filed the suit; EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin was named as a defendant.

The groups argued that repealing the finding and related vehicle safeguards violated the EPA’s responsibilities under the Clean Air Act. They cited prior court rulings recognizing the agency’s authority to regulate greenhouse gases. The EPA said it had reevaluated the legal foundation and argued Congress had not authorized the regulations at issue. The dispute therefore concerns both the agency’s statutory authority and the climate finding that underpinned federal rules.

The Guardian also reported a separate petition filed the same day by 18 young people, represented by Our Children’s Trust and Public Justice. That petition is distinct from the nonprofit lawsuit.

title: Trump nominates hospitality executive to lead National Park Service
description_short: Trump nominates hospitality executive to lead National Park Service
description_medium: Trump nominates hospitality executive to lead National Park Service. Scott Socha, whose company sued to claim trademark rights to Yosemite name, criticized by conservation groups This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long:
On February 12, 2026, Donald Trump nominated Scott Socha to lead the National Park Service. Socha had spent 27 years at Delaware North, a hospitality company that provides services in seven national parks and operates lodging in five nearby communities. The Guardian reported that he had overseen park-related business development since 2017. His nomination required Senate confirmation.

Conservation advocates criticized the choice because Socha’s experience was in hospitality rather than conservation or public service. Save Our Parks said he lacked conservation experience, while the Center for Western Priorities urged senators to scrutinize his record. Delaware North had also sued over trademark rights to Yosemite National Park, the Ahwahnee Hotel and Curry Village after losing a 2016 contract to operate Yosemite’s hotels and restaurants. The case settled in 2019, after the landmarks had briefly been renamed.

The nomination put a hospitality executive with concession-industry ties in line to lead the agency overseeing those public lands. The Guardian’s report records the advocates’ concerns and Socha’s business history but gives no detailed White House explanation for the selection.

title: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_short: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_medium: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds. YouGov poll shows 50% support as Kristi Noem defends ‘terrorist’ claim and shutdown drags on This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long:
An Economist/YouGov poll conducted February 27 through March 2, 2026, found that 50% of Americans somewhat or strongly supported abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, while 39% opposed it. YouGov said this was the first time support in its polling reached 50%. Support included 77% of Democrats and 52% of independents; 68% of Republicans opposed abolition, while 23% supported it. The Guardian placed the result amid the Trump administration’s enforcement operations and a partial Homeland Security shutdown.

The YouGov report also found that 75% favored requiring ICE officers to wear identifying uniforms and 59% opposed allowing agents to hide their faces with masks. It reported that 58% said ICE used excessive force and 44% said they had no confidence in the agency. These results show the poll measured views on agency abolition alongside specific enforcement practices and confidence in ICE.

The Guardian connected the polling to scrutiny of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem following the Minneapolis deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. The accessible YouGov article provides the response breakdown and support categories but not the sample size or full methodology, so those details remain unavailable.
